title: Reading hive sounds for colony health
subtitle: What the sound of a colony tells you before you open the hive.
excerpt: An experienced beekeeper can learn a great deal about a colony before lifting a single frame. The sound of the hive, from the low steady hum of a content colony to the roar of a queenless or disturbed one, is a first-line indicator of what you will find inside. Learning to read it reduces disturbance and speeds diagnosis.
sourceNotes: Ted Hooper, Guide to Bees and Honey (7th edn., 2010), colony assessment chapter. BBKA, Seasonal Beekeeping (2019). Thomas Seeley, Honeybee Democracy (2010), communication chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: A high-pitched tooting or quacking sound made by a virgin queen as she challenges other queens in the hive. Indicates a queen is present and the colony may swarm.
The loud, disorganised hum of a colony that has lost its queen. Distinct from the steady buzz of a queen-right colony.

content.text: Bees communicate through sound, vibration, and pheromone. The sounds audible to a beekeeper at the hive entrance or with an ear to the box fall into a small number of patterns. Learning these patterns gives you a useful pre-inspection read.

A queen-right colony on a warm day makes a steady, moderate hum, slightly irregular, with individual buzzes weaving in and out. If you put your ear to the hive wall, you hear this as a relaxed, multilayer sound. The bees are going about their business. This is the baseline you are comparing everything else to.

is louder and more disorganised than the content hum. The pitch is higher and the sound lacks the steady rhythm of a normal colony. Bees at the entrance may be fanning harder and the activity looks frantic rather than purposeful. If the hive sounds like this before disturbance, inspect for queen presence.

is a distinctive, repeating high note (tooot-tooot) heard from outside the hive or clearly when you rest a hand on the box. It means a virgin queen has emerged and is challenging other capped queens. If you hear piping, the colony is likely in a post-swarm state with an unmated queen. Do not inspect for 2 to 3 weeks; let the queen mate and return before disturbing the colony.

A colony that has been disturbed or that contains a more defensive population will go into a roaring, high-pitched alarm when you approach. The sound escalates sharply as soon as you touch the hive. This is not the same as the queenless roar: it starts from normal and rises with disturbance. Open cautiously with adequate smoke and work slowly.

In winter, hold a stethoscope to the hive wall to check whether the colony is alive without opening the box. A live cluster produces a faint but unmistakable hum. Silence for more than 10 seconds means the colony has likely died. Wait for a mild day (above 10 C) before opening to investigate.

attrs.cue: Hive is completely silent in April when it should be active
attrs.cause: Colony has died over winter, or has absconded
attrs.fix: Open on a mild day. Check for the remains of a cluster. No cluster, pollen stores still present, and empty cells with the outer frames still capped suggest starvation. Wax moth or varroa damage presents differently: look for chalkbrood, perforated capping, or mite debris on the floor.

attrs.cue: Constant high roar from a hive during a summer nectar dearth
attrs.cause: Robbing in progress: bees from other colonies attempting to steal stores
attrs.fix: Reduce the entrance to 2 to 3 cm immediately. Watch the entrance for bees fighting and bees trying to enter from the side of the hive. If robbing is severe, reduce to a 1-bee entrance and leave for 48 hours.
